title: Why the Bronze Age collapsed
summary: Sea Peoples, drought, earthquakes, revolt, or a fragile trade web? Weigh the evidence for each and see why historians now blame all of them.
objective: Judge which evidence supports which proposed cause of the Late Bronze Age collapse, spot inferences the evidence can't carry, and explain the systems-collapse view.
subject: history

source.title: Eric H. Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed

hook.prompt: Within roughly fifty years around 1200 BCE, Hattusa was emptied and burned, Mycenaean palaces fell, and Ugarit was destroyed. Which single cause do most historians today accept for all of it?

options.feedback: The best-attested suspect, but inland Hattusa is a poor fit for raiders from the sea, and the main source is one empire's victory monument.
Pollen cores support a dry phase, but the region had survived droughts before, and drought doesn't throw down citadel walls.
Crushed skeletons at Mycenae and Tiryns support quakes there, but the destructions span decades, not a day.

hook.explanation: Each cause has real evidence behind it and real sites it can't explain. The question isn't *which one* but *how do you weigh them*.

bricks.title: Five suspects and their evidence
bricks.body: Five causes are proposed. **Sea Peoples:** Ramesses III's Medinet Habu reliefs show land and sea battles; Ugarit's last letters report enemy ships. **Drought:** pollen cores from coastal Syria and Cyprus show a dry phase from about 1200 BCE; letters ask for grain. **Earthquakes:** collapsed walls and crushed bodies at Mycenae and Tiryns. **Internal revolt:** palaces burned, nothing foreign left behind. **Trade fragility:** bronze needed Cypriot copper and far-eastern tin; break one link and every palace suffers.

visual.alt: Table of five proposed causes, the main evidence for each, and what each fails to explain.

bricks.prompt: Match each piece of evidence to the cause it supports most directly.

pairs.left: Reliefs of a sea battle at Medinet Habu, year 8 of Ramesses III
Pollen cores from coastal Syria and Cyprus showing a dry phase from about 1200 BCE
Skeletons under collapsed walls at Mycenae and Tiryns
The Uluburun wreck: Cypriot copper, tin from the east, goods of many cultures

bricks.explanation: Each find is strong for one cause and silent on the others. The Uluburun wreck shows how far the bronze supply chain stretched, which made a cascade possible.

bricks.prompt: Three of these objections to "the Sea Peoples did it" hold up. Which one doesn't?

options.text: Hattusa lies far inland and seems to have been emptied before it burned; seaborne raiders fit it badly
options.feedback: This one holds. A planned evacuation is hard to square with a sack from the sea.

options.text: Egypt, which fought them, is the one great power that survived; the account is a victory monument
options.feedback: This one holds. A monument to Ramesses III's triumph has every reason to make the enemy look decisive.

options.text: "Sea Peoples" is a modern label; Egyptian texts list separate named groups such as the Peleset and Shekelesh
options.feedback: This one holds. The collective name is nineteenth-century, a reason not to picture one coordinated force.

options.text: No destruction layer shows foreign weapons or pottery, so the raids never happened

bricks.explanation: Missing foreign traces don't rule out raiders: Ugarit's letters describe enemy ships, and attackers who don't settle leave little behind. The other objections target what the Sea Peoples *can't* explain.

bricks.title: What a burnt layer can and can't say
bricks.body: A destruction layer shows a place burned, not who or what burned it. Historians read the details: bodies crushed under masonry point to earthquake; arrowheads in walls to fighting; archives and valuables removed first to a planned evacuation, as at Hattusa; local pottery above the ash to survivors returning rather than newcomers. Old stories get re-checked: Ugarit's tablets were long said to be baking in a kiln as the city fell; later study suggests they fell from an upper floor.

bricks.prompt: A site report for a hypothetical Late Bronze Age town. Tap the inference the evidence doesn't support.

visual.html:
Site report

Hypothetical Late Bronze Age town, destruction phase

  1. A thick ash layer seals the palace floors.
  2. Bronze arrowheads are embedded in the outer wall.
  3. The arrowheads show the town saw fighting.
  4. Two skeletons under fallen masonry show the attackers brought the walls down on residents.
  5. Local-style pottery above the ash suggests survivors or neighbours reoccupied the site.

bricks.explanation: Bodies under fallen masonry are what earthquakes leave, and nothing ties the arrowheads to the collapse. Fighting then a quake, or a quake then raiders, both fit.

bricks.prompt: Pollen cores from coastal Syria and Cyprus indicate a dry phase beginning about 1200 BCE and lasting roughly three centuries. What does this establish?

options.text: Drought is consistent with the timing, but the cores can't show it caused any particular city's fall
Drought was the main cause: the dates match
options.feedback: Matching dates are necessary, not sufficient. Core dating is coarse, the region had survived droughts before, and drought doesn't explain earthquake damage or an emptied-then-burned Hattusa.

options.text: Little: pollen records plants, not politics
options.feedback: Vegetation tracks rainfall, rainfall tracks harvests, and letters from the period ask for grain. The cores corroborate the texts.

options.text: It rules out the Sea Peoples
options.feedback: Drought and migration aren't rivals. A long drought is one of the better explanations for why people moved in the first place.

bricks.explanation: Timing and famine texts make drought a strong contributor. Blaming it for one city's fall needs site evidence, so most historians call it one stress among several.

bricks.title: Systems collapse: a perfect storm
bricks.body: Eric Cline's reading, now the mainstream one: no single cause explains every site, and it didn't have to. The Late Bronze Age powers were tightly coupled: bronze needed Cypriot copper and tin from far to the east, and Egypt shipped grain to a hungry Hatti. A system like that absorbs one shock. Within a few decades it took drought, earthquakes, raids, and revolt together, and each failure made the next more likely.

visual.alt: Copper from Cyprus, tin from the east, and grain from Egypt all feed the palace economies, while drought, earthquakes, raids, and revolt hit them at once.

bricks.prompt: Put one plausible systems-collapse cascade in order.

items.text: Drought cuts harvests across several regions
Palaces import grain; letters plead for shipments
Hungry populations move; raiders strike coastal cities
Sea routes become unsafe; copper and tin shipments stop
Without bronze or trade income, palaces can't pay or arm; centres are abandoned or burned

bricks.explanation: Each step removes the buffer that would have absorbed the next. The sequence differed by region, but the chain ran through the trade network, so coupled powers fell together.

bricks.prompt: Two explanations of the collapse. Which argues better from the evidence?

options.text: The Sea Peoples destroyed the Bronze Age world. Egypt's reliefs show them attacking, Ugarit's last letters describe enemy ships, and the great coastal cities fell within a generation.
options.feedback: Internally consistent, but it picks the coastal sites, reads a victory monument as a neutral record, and says nothing about inland Hattusa, the drought cores, or the earthquake damage.

options.text: No single cause fits every site. Hattusa was emptied before it burned, Mycenaean citadels show earthquake damage, pollen shows a long drought, and Ugarit's letters mention famine as well as raiders. Several stresses hit an interdependent network at once.

bricks.explanation: The many-causes explanation fits more of the evidence, including inland sites the Sea Peoples story ignores, and shows why the raids hit so hard: the system was already strained.

challenge.prompt: A new paper argues a single great earthquake destroyed Mycenae, Tiryns, Hattusa, and Ugarit in the same year. Which finding would most damage the claim?

options.text: Pottery and radiocarbon dates spread the destructions across several decades
The sites are up to a thousand kilometres apart
options.feedback: Suggestive, not decisive: that's exactly why the "earthquake storm" model proposes a series of quakes over decades. Only the dates separate one quake from many.

options.text: Egyptian records never mention an earthquake
options.feedback: Egypt wasn't struck, and silence in one archive is weak evidence either way.

options.text: Hattusa shows signs of evacuation before it burned
options.feedback: Damaging for Hattusa, but the paper could drop that one site and keep the rest. A finding that undercuts all four is stronger.

challenge.explanation: A single event can't span decades. That's why Nur and Cline framed the earthquake idea as a *storm*, a series over about fifty years, and still only one contributor.

takeaways: A destruction layer tells you a city ended; who or what ended it takes bodies, weapons, what was removed, and who came after.
The Sea Peoples are the best-attested suspect and the weakest single explanation: the account is a victory monument, and inland Hattusa fell too.
Drought cores and grain letters make climate a strong contributor, but matching dates aren't proof.
Most historians now favour systems collapse: several stresses hitting an interdependent trade network within a few decades.
